I took the gray purse with its jeweled crescent
And fastened it around my waist.
Making my army of six divisions obey,
I pursued Sarybay.
I overcame his giant champion;
Though crammed full of courage,
I stretched him lengthwise on the ground.
Whoever opposed me,
I split open upon the road.
I made the shooting furious
And the clash of battle fierce;
I exposed the champions
Of the infidel Sarybay’s host
And slaughtered their entire band.
I annihilated them completely,
All his many kinds of companions;
I bent his giants double with my spear
And drove the villain’s
Far-famed rage out of him.
Felling his forest, I made a road,
And brought his whole world to disgrace.
Hewing them down with the sword
And battering them with the spear,
I brought dreadful havoc upon them.
When the infidel, the monster’s son,
Stood there lamenting,
Saying, “My strength cannot overcome a woman,”
He seemed as though his father had died that day;
He burned with shame,
And his lion nature was revealed.
He began to scream and shriek,
Having lost his finest army.
I made my woman’s head a warrior’s
And tightly girded my waist.
I chased the earth-crushing swine
Away from Zhelpinish.
Saying, “This is how the conflict stood,”
I waged such a battle.
I felled his heroes,
Made his renowned men crawl,
And opened a road through the dead end.
I slaughtered every villain
Who boasted of being a champion, leaving them corpses;
I trampled beneath my feet
And humiliated his champion who charged the banner.
I seized the man he had posted as sentry
And made him a slave.
Without letting him turn his courser’s head
Or rise before the world,
I poured volleys upon him.
I crippled his champion
And struck him down in bewilderment;
Then I wheeled around and renewed the battle.
Saying, “This is the way of combat,”
I made my horse’s flanks stream with sweat.
Around all four corners of the world
I drove the villain who had descended upon you,
Circling him four times.
For six full days, without letting his back touch earth,
I gave him no freedom,
Allowed him no room upon the land,
And denied him his own will.
For two days I did not let him settle on the ground;
Such boundless havoc did I wreak.
I opened Zhelzhetpes to full speed,
And drove the earth-crushing swine
Out of Zhelpinish.
I tightly girded my waist
And leveled my spear along the ridge.
Neither by day nor by night did I cease;
I pursued the swine who had conquered China
And made sport of the chase.
I enslaved all his encamped household,
And his thoughts became black as night.
His violence became known among the people;
He could not find a handspan of ground,
Nor a grave to enter,
Nor a hollow in which to shelter,
Nor river water to plunge into,
Nor a village where he might encamp,
Nor any land to flee to.
I waged countless battles.
Strewing grass upon his yellow trail,
I pursued the infidel, the monster’s son,
Until he turned pale and wan.
Strewing grass upon his fleeing tracks,
I hounded him until his face went white.
Upon the swaggering swine
I brought a mighty conflict.
I tore the villain away
From the lord in whom he trusted
And from his secure stronghold.
Forcing the villain into submission,
I severed him from his people.
I slaughtered his strongest men;
Straddling his bravest,
I annihilated them utterly.
I trod upon their heads
And hacked their people apart alive.
I began a thousand conflicts
And slaughtered every last one
Of the men who showed courage.
The hillsides, bluffs, and valleys
Became the road I myself had cleared.
I had taken an army with me
To seize the villain, the monster’s son.
Unable to find the monster’s son,
I wore the backs of my horses raw.
I roamed all four corners
Of the world, circling them four times.
I opened my white charger to full speed,
Driving the villainous slave before me;
I couched my steel spear
And roamed over the earth,
Searching without rest for seven years.
His oppression has not abated;
He has besieged Zhylgyn, Keng-Kol, and Talas,
And his tyranny still lies upon them.
That bright pass with its lofty bluffs—
That is the road I cleared.
This is the army that fought
The infidel, the monster’s son;
This is the mouth that traded words with him.
I am the maiden Kuyaly, the champion—
I shall unleash a great conflict for the ages.
If I meet him face-to-face in combat,
Could Sarybay ever stand against me?
This was all I ever asked
Of almighty God.
Having blunted my steel
And destroyed Sarybay,
At the encampment pitched here since yesterday,
Where Kökmonchok, daughter of Beri,
Was holding her games,
I hobbled Zhelzhetpes beneath me
And tied him to graze.
I removed the saddle
From my courser and left him bareback;
Beneath the plane tree below,
I tethered him on a long lead to graze,
Quenched his thirst beyond the ridge,
And let him crop the lush grass.
I shod Zhan-Baspas,
And beneath me the charger Saykashka,
With shoes of gold.
Finding no mountain left to tread,
No enemy left to fight,
We hunted with clamor, raising dust,
Played on the swings, making merry,
Held maidens’ games to great acclaim,
And played bold games amid clouds of dust;
When bored, we hunted roe deer.
If the dear soul does not weary,
By the river stands a clustered poplar;
When they camped beside the clustered poplar,
When the revelry came into full bloom.
When the pale dawn broke,
When the constellation Libra vanished,
And sank behind the looming mountain,
When the cold wind of daybreak
Swept down the river,
When the pale dawn stood,
Stars glittered in the sky,
As the pale dawn opened,
And yesterday light spread over the earth,
Yesterday, noble Aichürök,
My days of honor had departed.
After Sarybai unleashed his wrath,
And ground Talas to dust,
After Sarybai laid siege to it,
Aichürök, Akun’s daughter,
Traversed the whole wide earth,
And wandered throughout the universe;
I drained away her sorrowful blood,
And aged her noble head.
Her heart pierced, she withdrew,
And from Sarybai’s wrath
Tears poured from her eyes;
Only a spoonful of blood remained,
Her fly-sized soul shrieked,
Unable to endure, she sobbed,
Her heart pierced by sorrow, she withdrew,
And tears poured from her eyes;
Her fly-sized soul shrieked,
Truly entering in, she was battered,
And pleaded with wretched me.
The reason for her pleading was—
The stars in heaven were dim,
And she, ill-fated like me,
Was my sworn friend unto the afterlife.
That accursed enemy Sarybai—
The swine’s cruelty has gone too far;
“Let there be a mighty exchange of shots,
And by Almighty God’s wrath
Deliver them,” she said.
God created him as a lion,
The doomed sultan Semetey,
Whose fortune was perfect.
If you looked into his heart,
It was broader than the earth.
Born of man and woman,
Such a dear lion was created but once;
His like could never be among mankind.
Take the sun-faced noble sultan
To be your husband.
Against the grievous foe Sarybai,
Wage the struggle with all your might.
From the hands of that savage dog,
Let Semetey’s Seytek
And Külchoro, son of Almambet,
Be delivered,” she said.
Chürök cried and wailed,
Speaking graceful, honeyed words,
And lamenting with bitter sobs.
From the spirits I heard the news
That my beloved Semetey
Was locked in enmity
With the hero, son of the ogre;
Of the fierce gunfire
I heard, and came to rescue him
From the magnanimous hero’s son.
In frantic haste I traveled,
Never resting by day,
Never taking a day’s repose,
Never lying down to ease my hips,
Never reclining to satisfy my sleep,
Crossing towering lofty mountains,
Wading through deep ravines,
Driving the horse relentlessly onward,
Crossing passes and treading stones,
Until at last I arrived and made camp.
When the horse grew as small as a lark,
In frantic haste I traveled,
And came through tumult and turmoil.
My beloved hero Sultan—
I have seen the bloodthirsty lion!
When sent ahead, he brought good fortune;
When riding behind, he equaled countless troops.
He wore a blue lynx-fur cap,
And wielded a mottled-blue shield;
He spared no soul who faced him.
His eyes saw from afar;
Amid a great assembly,
He emerged alone from the race.
The mightiest of saints,
The fortress of the blessed lion.
Precious elder Bakai,
A saint who knew the ages,
Your fortunate uncle Bakai—
Behold how great his dignity.
His blessing enriched the soul,
His worth brought radiance to life.
His word was never spoken twice,
And he watched over the whole universe.
